# Current state — legeos

What the project believes right now: live terms, constraints, policies and requirements, and what has been found or assessed. Decisions have their own view, `DECISION-HISTORY.md`.

## Terms

_(none)_

## Constraints

### The first release does not attempt a custom kernel, libc, package format/manager, display protocol, object filesystem, universal checkpointing, all NVIDIA generations, an app store, phone/tablet/server editions, or third-party shell extensions

`active` · `@legeos.constraint.first-release-scope/1` · scope `all` · topic `first-release-scope`

Until the five first-release claims are proven, LegeOS keeps systemd, cgroup v2, APT/Debian packages, standard filesystems, PipeWire, NetworkManager, BlueZ, Mesa and the upstream NVIDIA userspace stack. It does not build: a Linux kernel fork, a new package format or manager, a new libc/basic userland, replacement networking/Bluetooth/audio stacks, a new display protocol, a semantic/object filesystem replacing paths, transparent checkpointing of arbitrary applications, support for every old NVIDIA generation, a complete alternative application store, phone/tablet/server editions, or extensions/third-party shell plugins.

### Identity comes from the launch cgroup, never from a client's self-declared app_id; Exec= is never run through a shell; the governor is observe-only until traces are reviewed and never selects a victim by memory size alone

`active` · `@legeos.constraint.identity-and-launch-safety/1` · scope `path "crates/lege-appd/**"`, `path "crates/lege-window/**"`, `path "services/lege-resourced/**"` · topic `identity-launch-governor-safety`

(1) A window's application identity is resolved PID -> cgroup -> instance -> canonical AppId; client claims (Wayland app_id, WM_CLASS, sandbox id) can only lower confidence (claim mismatch) or, when unique, yield claim-only confidence — never override a verified launch, and privileged actions require verified-launch. (2) Applications are launched as the registered executable plus an argument vector in a dedicated systemd unit; Exec= lines are parsed, never passed to a shell. (3) lege-resourced ships observe-only; enforcement (memory.high, reclaim, checkpoint, cgroup.kill) is enabled in stages after recorded traces are reviewed; the victim score weighs growth, PSI contribution, foreground/visible state, unsaved work and disposability, never resident size alone; session-critical units are never candidates.

### LegeOS development and validation run in the native Lubuntu installation, not WSL

`active` · `@legeos.constraint.native-lubuntu-is-the-development-environment/1` · scope `all` · topic `development-environment`

The machine's native Lubuntu installation is the authoritative LegeOS development and validation environment. A Windows-hosted request may use WSL for agent-only helpers such as OptMem, but WSL results must not be treated as LegeOS build, test, packaging, runtime, hardware, or deployment evidence.

### Exactly one selected provider per exclusive system role may autostart

`active` · `@legeos.constraint.one-provider-per-role/1` · scope `path "crates/lege-session-core/src/autostart.rs"`, `path "crates/lege-session-core/src/providers.rs"`, `path "crates/lege-types/src/provider.rs"` · topic `one-provider-per-role`

For every ProviderRole (network-status-ui, notification-server, file-chooser, file-manager, lock-screen, association-broker, clipboard-manager, power-manager, screenshot-service, input-method, portal-backend, greeter) installing a second provider never silently starts both; the user or distribution policy selects one and only that one autostarts.

### Every component is a Debian package (nothing under /usr/local or untracked in $HOME); lege-window carries no async runtime or D-Bus dependency

`active` · `@legeos.constraint.packaging-and-render-thread/1` · scope `path "crates/lege-window/**"`, `path "debian/**"`, `path "tools/xtask/**"` · topic `packaging-and-render-thread`

All binaries, units, manifests and policy files are installed by Debian packages (cargo-deb now, the vendored source package later); development installs go through a local apt repository. The compositor-side lege-window crate must never depend on tokio, zbus, async-std or smol because it runs on the compositor render thread.

### System behaviour belongs in services; tray icons, panels and applets are views

`active` · `@legeos.constraint.services-not-indicators/1` · scope `path "crates/lege-session-core/**"`, `path "services/**"`, `path "shell/**"` · topic `services-not-indicators`

No policy (timezone discovery, power decisions, autostart choices, association defaults, notification storage) is implemented in a shell surface or applet; each lives in a service crate/daemon with a D-Bus interface, and the shell only renders and forwards user choices.

## Observations

### The live watcher never refreshed a directory's own metadata when its contents changed, so folders showed modification times from before their contents changed

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.a-directory-whose-contents-changed-kept-a-stale-modification-time/1` · scope `path "crates/lege-file-index/src/btrfs_delta.rs"`, `path "crates/lege-file-index/src/mutation.rs"`, `path "crates/lege-file-index/src/watch.rs"`

Three of the four Btrfs correctness-gate failures were bugs in shared index code that the delta merely exercised, and two of those were live on the inotify watcher's own path, where they had gone unnoticed because the watcher's tests compared namespaces and not metadata. (1) A write through one name of a hard link left the index's other names holding stale size and mtime; the watcher reaches this through IN_MODIFY on a linked file. Fixed by mirroring a write to an inode's other names, gated on nlink > 1 so the common case costs one probe on entries_object. (2) A move onto an already-occupied path aborted the batch with UNIQUE constraint failed: entries.root_id, entries.path_bytes; the watcher reaches this through rename(2) over an existing destination, which is what every editor's atomic save does. Fixed by having the move take the occupant's row over. (3) The largest one: a directory whose entries changed never had its own metadata re-read, so its mtime and ctime in the index were from before its contents changed — a folder in a file manager showing a modification time older than the files it contains. inotify names the child; nothing tells the index the parent's own mtime moved. Found by upgrading tests/watch.rs to the same field-for-field metadata comparison the delta harness uses, which failed immediately with exactly one differing row in each nested-rename test: the directory the rename happened in. Fixed by having WatchOwner::pump re-read a directory that gained or lost an entry, one extra lstat per pump, so unpacking 10,000 files into a directory costs one stat rather than 10,000. The same metadata upgrade also caught a retarget_subtree path with a trailing separator from Path::join(""), equal to its sibling for every Path comparison but a different byte string as an index key; six hand-written test streams describing sequences no kernel emits, which had been passing by agreeing with each other rather than with the filesystem; and one unit test that asserted the mtime bug outright. There is now a single metadata-comparison definition (crates/lege-file-index/tests/support/entry_facts.rs) shared by the Btrfs harness, the delta unit tests and the watcher tests, so the asymmetry that hid all of this cannot reopen. The general lesson is that a namespace-only comparison cannot see a whole class of index defect, and the delta lane's value was not confined to the backend it was measuring.

> **Stale** — `watches "crates/lege-file-index/src/watch.rs"` was matched by `0c236928`, which touched `crates/lege-file-index/src/watch.rs`. See [REVIEW-REQUIRED.md](REVIEW-REQUIRED.md#the-live-watcher-never-refreshed-a-directorys-own-metadata-when-its-contents-changed-so-folders-showed-modification-times-from-before-their-contents-changed).

### A consumer had no way to learn the change-log position its snapshot was taken at

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.a-snapshot-did-not-say-which-change-position-it-was-consistent-with/2`

`SnapshotManifest` carried no sequence, so a consumer synchronising a subscription had to call `changes_since(0, 1)` after taking the snapshot and read `next_seq` — two calls, with everything committed between them landing in neither the frame nor the stream. That is exactly the read/subscribe race @legeos.decision.event-driven-service-authorities forbids. Worse, the workaround does not survive its own success: once the bounded change log has been pruned, sequence 0 is below the retained floor and `changes_since(0, …)` answers `SnapshotRequired` rather than a position, so a consumer that fell behind could not resnapshot its way back either. Found by writing the contract as one consumer-shaped sequence (`crates/lege-file-index/tests/consumer_contract.rs`) rather than as separate unit tests, each of which passed. Fixed by `SnapshotManifest.snapshot_seq`, read inside `write_snapshot` before the rows and serde-defaulted so no signature changes.

### A Trash1 smoke test run against the real session bus emptied the user's actual volume trash

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.agent-smoke-test-emptied-a-real-volume-trash/1` · scope `path "cli/lege/**"`, `path "services/lege-filed/**"`

While smoke-testing `lege trash empty --yes` end to end, the implementing agent constructed TrashApi with TrashMounts::System instead of TrashMounts::Fixed, so the sweep read the machine's real mount table, found /media/dk/4668959A68958977/.Trash-1000, and permanently deleted its one entry — a folder named `target` (a Rust build directory, regenerable) trashed on 2026-08-30. Unrecoverable. The code behaved as designed; the harness choice was the fault: TrashMounts::Fixed exists precisely so tests cannot reach real disks, every committed test uses it, and the offending smoke script was removed rather than left as a trap. Standing rule going forward: any end-to-end exercise of destructive file operations must run against fixture mounts (TrashMounts::Fixed, a throwaway HOME and XDG_DATA_HOME) — never the developer host's real mount table.

### A user can take the read-only checkpoints but cannot send the delta between them, so the delta backend is split across the privilege boundary

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.btrfs-send-needs-privilege-but-snapshotting-does-not/2` · scope `path "services/lege-hostd/src/index_checkpoint.rs"`

Probed on a loopback Btrfs fixture with the declared LegeOS subvolume layout (@, @home, @var, @snapshots, @deployments), kernel 6.17, btrfs-progs 6.16, by running scripts/btrfs-index-fixture.sh probe as root and comparing against the same operations run as uid 1000. As the unprivileged owner of the subvolume: btrfs subvolume snapshot -r succeeds, and a second read-only snapshot succeeds. btrfs send --no-data -p fails, and btrfs subvolume delete fails, the latter despite the filesystem being mounted with user_subvol_rm_allowed. Run as root the same send produced 450 bytes of metadata delta, confirming the operation itself is sound and only the privilege is missing. The consequence for the architecture is that the delta backend cannot live wholly in the per-user lege-filed: taking a checkpoint could, but producing the delta between two of them requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN and must go through lege-hostd, as must discarding a spent checkpoint. That in turn forces the transport question, because the stream lege-hostd writes is mode 0600 and root-owned while the daemon that must read it runs as the user, and a metadata delta names every path under @home so it must not be made world-readable.

### A press just below a framed window's visible bottom-right corner lands on Close; the resize corner is a whole tag height lower

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.close-tag-sits-under-the-client-bottom-right-corner/1`

Read from the code at 50af378. A framed window's frame is its client plus a TAG_HEIGHT (32) strip below it: WindowService::client_area (crates/templar-window/src/service.rs:1130) returns geometry::client_area(frame), which subtracts the strip from the bottom (geometry.rs:504-511), and tag_strip (geometry.rs:405-414) is the frame's bottom 32 rows. chrome::layout::control_tags (compositor/templar-comp/src/chrome/layout.rs:220-244) packs Park, Maximize, Close against the strip's right edge, so Close is the 32x32 square directly beneath the client's bottom-right 32 pixels. press_target_at (compositor/templar-comp/src/input.rs:276-311) tests a point inside the frame against the control tags before anything else, and resize_edges_at (geometry.rs:544-580) answers only outside the frame, so the bottom-right resize corner begins at frame.bottom(), 32 px below the corner the person can see. A press aimed at the visible bottom-right corner from below or a little inside therefore closes the window; one aimed at the bottom-left corner grabs the name tag (a move or a pin). Inferred from code reading, not reproduced with a pointer; no test in the tree presses the visible client corners through press_target_at.

### Nested, the machine cluster once received no pointer events while its input region was declared; the measurement was confounded and the user verifies it by hand

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.cluster-pointer-delivery-with-an-input-region-is-unverified/1` · scope `path "compositor/templar-comp/src/input.rs"`, `path "shell/templar-shell/src/surface/cluster_screen.rs"`, `path "shell/templar-shell/src/wayland_bridge.rs"`

During the task-system campaign's nested checks, Lane C measured that the bottom-right cluster received no pointer events while wl_surface.set_input_region was declared with the correct chip rectangles [(8,8,112,32),(128,8,96,32),(232,8,160,32),(400,8,140,32)] on a 548x48 surface, and received them when the call was skipped; the island, which declares no region, delivered either way. The earlier ~25-30 px input/paint offset report was an artefact of measuring X screen coordinates against output coordinates. The user reports that during those runs they were using the machine and two other sessions were driving the pointer at once, so the hit-test result is most likely confounded, not a defect; Smithay's RendererSurfaceState::contains_point and RegionAttributes::contains read correctly for these rectangles. Unverified either way. What changed in this campaign around it: 186ae89 declares the input region on every present (previously only on the masked path, so a plain present kept the previous frame's region); 6d7943f makes the compositor re-run pointer motion when the surface under a resting pointer moves or resizes; 3703344 deletes the shell's follow_bottom_anchored_resize compensation. The user's hands-on gate: hover the bottom-right chips nested with nothing else driving the pointer, click the account chip, and drag the sliders; if the cluster does not react, the one-line suspect is declare_input_region in wayland_bridge.rs. Rule learned the hard way: never drive synthetic X input (xdotool) on this machine while it is in use; a nested check's clicks landed on the live browser.

### btrfs send --no-data is flat in tree size and proportional to the change, and the delta beats a crawl by up to 647x

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.delta-catch-up-cost-tracks-the-change-and-beats-a-crawl-except-on-bulk-creation/5` · scope `path "crates/lege-file-index/src/btrfs_delta.rs"`

The final measurement, run as root against a loopback Btrfs fixture on 2026-09-04 at commit 8d74542, across three tree sizes and eight scenarios, with the correctness gate passing for the first time. The architectural question this lane existed to answer was whether btrfs send itself is proportional to the change rather than to the tree, because a send proportional to the tree reduces the whole idea to a cheaper crawl. It is flat. The same change sent between snapshots of trees two orders of magnitude apart costs: nothing at all, 1.6 / 1.7 / 1.9 ms with a byte-identical 113 B stream; a whole-directory rename (4 paths), 2.4 / 2.4 / 2.8 ms, 481 B; an hour of desktop use (67 paths), 4.1 / 5.5 / 5.9 ms, 13.6 KiB; 100 new files (102 paths), 3.7 / 5.8 / 7.0 ms, 34.0 KiB; a build burst (7,007 paths), 128.7 / 148.7 / 149.3 ms, 2.7 MiB; one 1 GiB file (2 paths), 20.7 / 29.2 / 20.3 ms, 408.4 KiB. Stream size is identical across tree sizes in every row; residual send drift across a hundredfold tree is under 4 ms. Send is proportional to the change instead: at 153,327 entries, 1.9 ms at 0 changed paths, 2.8 at 4, 5.9 at 67, 7.0 at 102, 149.3 at 7,007 and 1,185.4 at 50,003 — roughly 24 microseconds per changed path above a 2 ms floor. End to end at 153,327 entries: an hour of desktop use 30.4 ms against 19,657.6 (647x), 100 new files 37.8 against 19,198.3 (508x), a whole-directory rename 49.4 against 19,577.1 (396x), truncate-chmod-rewrite 46.8 against 16,865.9 (361x), one 1 GiB file 39.1 against 11,329.3 (290x), nothing at all 71.1 against 17,588.2 (248x), a build burst 1,269.1 against 18,636.6 (15x), a mass delete of 50,003 rows 6,095.2 against 14,202.7 (2.3x). The two weak rows are the architecture working, not failing: the build burst is slower than a crawl only on the 1,540-entry tree (0.4x) and barely ahead at 15,339 (1.3x), a crossover of a few thousand entries that no real home reaches, and 2,001 of its paths were excluded by coverage policy before reaching the index; the mass delete's 2.3x is 4,910 of its 6,095 ms spent writing 50,003 tombstones, which the crawl arm pays too. --no-data holds for large files but scales with extents rather than bytes: a 1 GiB file yields 408.4 KiB in 8,200 commands, about one UPDATE_EXTENT per 128 KiB extent, so a dormant window writing 100 GiB costs on the order of 40 MiB of stream and there should be a cap above which the backend gives up and asks for a reconcile. The delta arm reads 0 block-layer bytes in all 24 rows against the crawl's 116-159 MiB, with the caveat that read_bytes is /proc/self/io of the harness process and btrfs send is a child, so the send's own reads are unmeasured; its 5.9 ms wall time bounds them to a few MiB. The full table is docs/measurements/btrfs-delta-measured.md, written by the harness. This supersedes revision 3, whose figures came from the third of five runs, before the last two correctness bugs were fixed.

### The 2026-10-01 desktop freeze stalled the display path while the machine kept running; the logs cannot say where

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.desktop-freeze-20261001-display-path-stall-machine-alive/2`

Boot a2228e0a709d40509c284f6698e0feb2 (2026-10-01 00:19:11 to 01:40:32 UTC, laptop with Intel Iris Xe driving eDP-1 and an RTX 4060 the compositor ignores) ended in a desktop freeze: display and pointer stopped, the user restarted the machine. Evidence available to the desktop user (user journal only; the account is not in adm, so kernel and system-unit lines were unreadable): templar-comp's last line was 01:26:59.226 (a 1x33 toplevel mapped and destroyed); after it, 962 entries from other processes, templar-resourced ticking every second with a largest gap of 1.002 s over the whole boot and level=normal from 01:00:50 on (MemAvailable about 28 GiB at the last level change), Firefox writing its profile until 01:40:19 and an agent session working until 01:34:05. At 01:40:30.698 the user manager began an orderly stop (Activating special unit exit.target); templar-comp took 1.450 s to stop against 0.15-0.19 s in boots -2 and -3 and logged nothing while stopping. templar-comp used 9 min 59 s CPU over 4881 s (12.3 percent), the same rate as healthy boots (11.8-12.2 percent), which rules out a full-core busy loop longer than about a minute. No idle blank was logged (the deployed build logs one), /var/lib/systemd/pstore is empty, systemd-coredump was not installed. Classification: a stall confined to the display path (templar-comp, or the i915 GPU/display work it waits on), not a whole-machine kernel lockup, memory exhaustion or OOM; whether templar-comp's main thread was blocked in a DRM/GPU wait or deadlocked, or its loop was alive with a page flip that never completed, is not decidable from what was logged. At the time templar-comp had no watchdog, kernel.sysrq was 176 (no W/L dumps), kernel.panic 0 and core_pattern `core`.

### Three 2026-10-01 freezes: templar-comp stopped presenting, kernel clean; loop stall vs dead render chain still open

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.desktop-freezes-20261001-compositor-main-thread-blocked/2`

Three desktop freezes on 2026-10-01, all on the installed build set b919ed4 (templar-comp without the watchdog): boots a2228e0a (comp silent from 01:26:59, power key 01:40:30), 54b1efc8 (comp silent from 06:39:02, power key 06:56:34) and a063f873 (comp silent from 07:26:05, power key 07:54:14). Read as root (scripts/freeze-evidence-setup.sh): every kernel log is clean in the freeze windows — no i915 error, GPU HANG, flip_done timeout, hung task (hung_task_timeout_secs 120, warnings left), lockup or OOM; logind records a short power-key press each time. templar-comp logged nothing for 13.5, 17.5 and 28 minutes while resourced ticked every second and filed, kitty and agent sessions kept working. In a063f873 templar-comp used 80.7 s CPU over 2219 s against about 12 percent of a core in healthy minutes: about 63 s before 07:26 and about 1 percent afterwards, so it was not spinning. Two faults remain open and the logs cannot separate them: the main thread blocked in an interruptible wait, or the loop alive but its vblank-driven render chain dead (no frame callbacks, so every client stops drawing too). The missing idle-blank and bar-claim lines do not decide it: input re-arms the idle timer and the shell's claims may wait on frame callbacks. The working tree now carries the evidence for both: the event-loop and page-flip watchdog, a repaint check that logs and restarts an output with nothing rendered, nothing in flight and no retry pending, a one-time needs_sync report and a slow-frame log; TEMPLAR_COMP_WATCHDOG_ABORT_AFTER_SECS=30 is set in the user's drop-in.

**supersedes** `@legeos.observation.desktop-freezes-20261001-compositor-main-thread-blocked/1`

### fanotify refuses a filesystem mark on a Btrfs subvolume, and one group cannot hold marks on two subvolumes at all — so it cannot cover LegeOS's declared layout

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.fanotify-cannot-span-btrfs-subvolumes/2` · scope `path "crates/lege-fanotify/**"`, `path "distro/deploy/layout.toml"`

fanotify_test_fsid in fs/notify/fanotify/fanotify_user.c (Linux v6.17) returns -EXDEV for a dentry whose statfs fsid differs from its superblock root's — the kernel comment names Btrfs subvolumes explicitly — and grants the weak-fsid fallback only when mark_type == FAN_MARK_INODE. FAN_MARK_FILESYSTEM and FAN_MARK_MOUNT therefore cannot mark @home, and distro/deploy/layout.toml:44 declares @, @home, @var, @snapshots and @deployments, all subvolumes. Independently, fanotify_set_mark_fsid refuses to hold weak-fsid marks from two different Btrfs subvolumes in one group, and one EventSource is one group — so even the unprivileged inode-mark variant could not watch @home and @ together, which inotify has no trouble with. The same weak-fsid guard was reproduced on this ext4/tmpfs/fuse host, where the fuse project drive reports fsid [0,0] (also weak): marking it in a group that already holds a tmpfs or ext4 mark returns EXDEV, and so does the reverse order, while two strong fsids (tmpfs then ext4) mix freely. Consequence for this machine: the 172,681-directory fuse project drive can be watched by a fanotify group only if that group watches nothing else. The FAN_MARK_FILESYSTEM path itself needs CAP_SYS_ADMIN and is not directly measured here; scripts/fanotify-privileged-probe.sh collects that one privileged step for the user to run against Lane E's Btrfs loopback fixture.

**supersedes** `@legeos.observation.fanotify-cannot-span-btrfs-subvolumes/1` · **verified_by** `@legeos.evidence.stale-observation-triage-20260908/1`

### After the 2026-10-01 freezes the evidence harness is armed on the laptop but the installed templar-comp still has no watchdog

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.freeze-watchdog-not-deployed-20261001/3`

Read from Lubuntu on 2026-10-01 against the TemplarOS root (/media/dk/templaros-root, journal @var/log/journal/13ddaed3..., readable via its ACL). Boot fbbc3d53 (2026-10-01 08:38-11:45 UTC) froze: after a logout at 09:04:24 (shell-initiated session restart) and a clean wake from a 900 s idle blank at 11:43:33, the user ran apt in kitty at 11:43:56-11:44:23, then clicked a window's tag; the display froze and they pressed the power key at 11:45:30 (the user's report; the journal alone reads like an orderly power-key poweroff, which is how every freeze so far has ended). Armed on the installed root: /usr/lib/sysctl.d/60-templaros-hang-evidence.conf, /usr/lib/systemd/journald.conf.d/60-templaros.conf, coredump.conf.d/templaros.conf, systemd-coredump, dk in adm; ~/.config/systemd/user/templar-comp.service.d/watchdog-abort.conf sets TEMPLAR_COMP_WATCHDOG_ABORT_AFTER_SECS=30. ### The Home chrome campaign 3 retired, and what took over each part

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.home-chrome-retired-to-the-bar-and-the-garden/1`

Campaign 3 splits one surface into two along a rule that had never been written down: Home
deals with your stuff, the bar deals with the machine (docs/garden/garden.md). Everything Home
carried that was about the machine, or about windows rather than about work, left it. This is
the record of what went and where it went, because five active work records describe a Home
that no longer exists in those parts and would otherwise read as current.

Retired from the Home Field, and its successor:

* The top-left "Home" plate and the top-right Help button in draw_search_bar. Help is still
  reachable by F1 and by the field context-menu row (field.help); Home is reached by the bar's
  new Home chip (home.reveal) and by Super. Successor: the bar's Home chip.
* The information row's live/parked window count in draw_information_row. Counting windows is
  the bar's job now. Successor: the taskbar, which shows the windows themselves.
* ParkedSession and WindowGroup tiles. merge_sessions and merge_window_groups no longer place a
  tile for any running, parked or grouped window, and a migration removes the ones already on
  existing fields as ordinary Remove ops, so undo and the document's invariants are untouched.
  Successor: the bar's taskbar, with parked entries dimmed.
* The three system widget tiles - session, notifications, settings - which merge_system no
  longer places, removed from existing fields by the same migration. That migration sweeps
  seven probe names (battery, volume, brightness, launcher, session, notifications, settings),
  not three, because a field written by an older generation of the shell can still be carrying
  the ones consolidated before this. The WidgetDescriptors stay in the shell's widgets module
  inert, marked as such, rather than being deleted: they are the only written record of the
  widget contract and the campaign did not test deleting them.
  Successors: session, settings and the sound/battery/brightness readings become the bar's
  machine cluster at the right end - one readings chip (battery, volume, brightness), network,
  clock, and an account chip whose popover carries settings.open and the five session.* actions.
  Notifications becomes the transient toast that already exists (ensure_toast on the
  notification layer), plus an unread chip on the bar when one is built.

What Home keeps is the Apps field, Files, Desktop, pinned objects and the garden. What "Home
shows your stuff" now means in the ledger is legeos.work.homegarden-phases-0-3.

Two premises are reversed rather than refined, and that is the part worth noticing: both
legeos.work.home-field and legeos.work.home-input-and-refinement commit in their titles to a
taskbar-free desktop, and campaign 3 has a taskbar. It is not the dock those records removed -
it is a bar of running windows grouped by the garden's own groups, which is a thing that could
not have been designed before the garden existed. The records stand for everything else they
did; this note is what stops them being read as current on this one point.

### Home's three-second refresh profiled: what was fixed, and the two service-side costs that remain

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.home-refresh-costs-profiled-20260902/2` · scope `path "services/lege-sessiond/src/apis/audio.rs"`, `path "services/lege-sessiond/src/apis/lifecycle.rs"`, `path "shell/lege-shell/**"`

Measured against a live sessiond on the development host, one pass of the Home Surface's three-second refresh loop cost about 82ms, of which: fetch_apps 34ms, fetch_settings_widget 19ms, fetch_session_widget 18ms, fetch_all(20) 5.5ms, fetch_projects 2.6ms, fetch_browser_sources 0.8ms. Separately, zbus's Connection::session() builds a new connection — socket, SASL handshake, Hello and a reader task — on every call, and the shell called it from three dozen places; caching one connection per tokio runtime took fetch_all from 14ms to 5.5ms.

Fixed in 392bd0d and f148046: the connection cache, joining the loop's independent fetches, joining the Session widget's three logind Can* questions (18ms to 13ms), and moving the application-catalogue read onto AppIdentity1.ApplicationsChanged plus a thirty-second backstop. An ordinary tick is now about 27ms.

Two costs remain and both are inside lege-sessiond, not the shell. Audio1.Get spawns `wpctl` as a child process on every call, which is most of fetch_settings_widget's remaining time; the Home Settings widget therefore spawns a process every three seconds for as long as the session lasts. Lifecycle1's Can* answers still cost about 13ms even when the three are asked together, which suggests the system-bus round trips to logind are being serialised inside sessiond rather than by the caller; logind's answer to whether this machine may shut down does not change between two three-second ticks and is a candidate for caching.

### Phase 4 half-day: Homegarden grew only the Desktop tray, fed by Home's own chrome; the terminal hook never ran and the Garden Clock never accumulated

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.homegarden-half-day-grew-only-the-desktop-tray-20260909/1`

After a half day in the LegeOS session on the Lubuntu host, the persisted ledger (session.db home_garden) held one context, /home/dk/Desktop, at Expanded (score 24) with buckets only launched-here (file-manager/terminal) and directory-opened; the sessiond journal showed 11 garden observations, all rooted at /home/dk/Desktop, zero terminal-entered, zero file-opened, zero project-entered. Four causes, none host-specific: (1) session/profile.d/60-legeos-garden.sh is read only by login shells and kitty on Linux never starts one (its login wrapper is macOS-only), so terminal-entered has never fired; the CLI test sources the script directly and is a false green. (2) Home's chrome is the only feed: the Desktop tray is the one Folder tile Home creates itself (field_model.rs merge_desktop_folder), its roles row launches kitty/pcmanfm --directory ~/Desktop which returns as launched-here, and every paint of a folder window pushes BrowseFolder which observes directory-opened once per shell process. (3) GardenClock accumulates active_ms only on Locked/Sleeping edges; logout emits none, so the persisted clock read {session 7, active_ms 0}; hours_since is identically 0, both demotion legs can never hold, and once Expanded a place stays Expanded. (4) /mnt/Samsung980_1TB/Rust-projects/.git exists, so attribute_root takes the highest marked ancestor and every repository under it would collapse into one Place. The 'little widget with 3 links' is paint_place at the Wide rung: name, state line, PLACE_ROLES chips, one branch row. Lane reports: .agent/scratch/homegarden-5/{A,B,C}-result.md.

### legeos.observation.hostd-hands-a-privileged-fd-through-deltaopen

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.hostd-hands-a-privileged-fd-through-deltaopen/2`

lege-hostd can now hand a privileged file descriptor to the per-user session daemon, through
one narrow purpose-built method rather than a general facility.
org.legeos.Host.IndexCheckpoint1.DeltaOpen returns `stream` as type="h" — the first type="h"
argument on any org.legeos.Host.* interface, which is precisely what
@legeos.question.no-route-for-a-privileged-fd-to-reach-the-per-user-daemon recorded as absent.
The call is polkit-gated on org.legeos.host.index-checkpoint
(services/lege-hostd/src/api.rs:307 and siblings; distro/policy/polkit/org.legeos.host.policy:71).
hostd writes the btrfs send stream, opens it, and unlinks it before returning, so the bytes
reach exactly one caller and no path survives the call: a metadata delta names every path under
@home, which is why the written file is 0600 root-owned and why the path form of Delta is not
usable by an unprivileged consumer. The interface's own comment frames this as the pattern
org.legeos.Files.Index1.OpenSnapshot already used on the session bus, with only the bus being
new. The receiving daemon never widens its privilege: it gets a read handle to a stream it could
not have produced, and nothing else. The fanotify half of the same question was not unblocked by
this route; it was declined on merit by
@legeos.decision.inotify-remains-the-index-event-backend, which keeps inotify as the index's
event backend and ships fanotify behind EventSource as a measured, unadopted alternative.

### hostd stages candidate deployments under /var/lib/templaros/hostd/deployments, not the @deployments/{id} that layout.toml and the provisioner declare

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.hostd-stages-candidates-outside-the-declared-deployments-subvolume/1`

At 50af378. distro/deploy/layout.toml:89 declares subvolume_template = "@deployments/{id}" and installer/provision.sh (fstab block around :1219-1231) mounts @deployments at /.deployments. templar-hostd's real configuration sets deployments_dir: state_dir.join("deployments") with state_dir = root/var/lib/templaros/hostd (services/templar-hostd/src/main.rs:47,65), i.e. inside the shared @var subvolume, and UpdateLedger::candidate_deployment uses candidate_dir(id).display() as the Deployment's subvolume (services/templar-hostd/src/updates.rs:374-378), which the boot-entry writers put into rootflags=subvol=. Only fixture tests use @deployments/{id}. [INFERENCE, not run on hardware] a staged candidate's entry would name subvol=/var/lib/templaros/hostd/deployments/<id>, a path relative to the mounted root rather than to the btrfs top level (where it is @var/lib/...), so the candidate would not boot; and a candidate kept in @var lives in the same subvolume as the persistent state it is supposed to be independent of. Separately, templar dev deploy keeps its own rollback snapshot at /var/lib/templaros/snapshots/root-before-<set> (cli/templar/src/dev/gates.rs:278-284), a second rollback location.

### Identity never resolves in a nested session, so the fan, the chip count, grouping and the launcher's running count can only be seen offscreen or on hardware

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.identity-never-resolves-in-a-nested-session/1` · scope `path "crates/templar-window/src/task.rs"`, `path "shell/templar-shell/src/taskbar.rs"`

Windows launched through `templar app launch` inside the nested session arrive with verified_identity false (identity is the cgroup's, and the nested session has no per-app cgroup), so task::units gives each window its own Unknown unit and never merges two windows of one application. Every island behaviour that depends on a unit with more than one window (the fan, the count badge, within-unit switching, the launcher's 'N running') is therefore invisible nested; it is exercised by the offscreen fan render and by the user's hands-on on hardware, and nothing else.

Idle-cost headline number measured as a real before/after pair across commit 6522e10 (an idle index watcher sleeps rather than wakes twice a second): watcher-thread schedstat pcount and voluntary_ctxt_switches over a 60s idle window went from 121/120 (pre-fix, built from worktree at be57fad) to 0/0 (post-fix, HEAD). 100k-entry workload suite: initial index 28,389 entries/s, warm 100-result search p50 0.96ms/p95 1.27ms, snapshot of 90,152 entries in 1.28s (12.2MB). 2,000,000-entry case not run (harness supports it via --allow-two-million --release; left for a follow-up). Full detail: docs/measurements/index-baseline-2026-09-04.md.

### The index consumer library links rusqlite transitively, so a dependency check cannot stand in for the no-shared-store rule

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.lege-client-links-rusqlite-through-the-shared-index-types/1`

`cargo tree -p lege-client -i rusqlite` succeeds: lege-client depends on lege-file-index, which depends on rusqlite. The link is real but it is a *linkage*, not a store access — `crates/lege-client/src/tree_source.rs` uses only the crate's `model`, `query` and `snapshot` types, and no consumer path opens a database. Separating those types from the store means feature-gating rusqlite out of lege-file-index and editing `crates/lege-client/Cargo.toml`, `cli/lege/Cargo.toml`, `crates/lege-fanotify/Cargo.toml` and `tools/xtask/Cargo.toml`, which this campaign did not do. So the `file-index-contract` acceptance check is satisfied by `crates/lege-file-index/tests/consumer_contract.rs` — which drives every read through snapshot and `changes_since` and never through `Index::open` — and not by a dependency-graph command that would have to be reported as failing when it passes.

### legeos.observation.memory-baseline-before-templaros-20260909

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.memory-baseline-before-templaros-20260909/1`

A memory baseline to compare TemplarOS against once it boots from its own partition, taken on the machine that will be replaced.

Measured with scripts/memory-snapshot.sh, which exists so the two readings mean the same thing: it uses only /proc/meminfo and per-process /proc/*/smaps_rollup, never a desktop-specific tool. It reports PSS rather than RSS, because RSS counts a shared library once per process that maps it and summing it over a session comes out larger than the machine has.

2026-09-09, host dk-82y3, 31815 MiB total, Linux 6.17.0-41-generic:

  MemTotal - MemAvailable   4921 MiB    in use, excluding reclaimable cache
  TOTAL PSS, this user      2941 MiB    over 62 processes
  DESKTOP TOTAL PSS          218 MiB    compositor 48, shell 43, filed 109, sessiond 13, resourced 5

The 218 MiB is the figure worth comparing; the other two are dominated by whatever happened to be open. What it is NOT is a Lubuntu figure: XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP was LegeOS, so this is the project's own desktop running on a Lubuntu 25.10 base, and an LXQt number needs somebody to log into an LXQt session. It is also a floor rather than a ceiling — hostd runs as root on the system bus and its smaps_rollup cannot be read by the desktop user — and it was not taken at idle: Firefox, Claude Code, kitty and an MCP server were running and the machine had just built an ISO, so Buffers+Cached is build output.

To make the comparison honest, take both readings the same way: freshly logged in, nothing else open, a few minutes after the session settles.

### legeos.observation.one-developer-tool-froze-the-machine-for-45-minutes-20260908

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.one-developer-tool-froze-the-machine-for-45-minutes-20260908/1`

On 2026-09-08 a single developer tool made the reference laptop unusable for 45 minutes, and
nothing on the system intervened. Measured at the time, not reconstructed: one rust-analyzer
process, spawned by an editor session indexing the Rust trees under
/mnt/Samsung980_1TB/Rust-projects, held 19.9 GB RSS — 61.2% of the machine's 31 GB — after 51
minutes. Swap was fully exhausted at 7.8 GiB of 7.8 GiB with 1.7 MiB free, free memory was
520 MiB, and the 15-minute load average was 57.89. Killing that one process returned free
memory from 520 MiB to 20 GiB and swap from 7.8 GiB to 2.8 GiB used, immediately: the machine
had not been computing, it had been servicing page faults.

The signature was visible in a build long before anyone read it as one. A cargo test run in the
AKR checkout reported 30 minutes wall with 2.4 seconds of user time and 27 minutes of system
time. A 675-to-1 sys-to-user ratio is not a slow compile; it is thrashing, and it was the
machine already dying.

What matters for LegeOS is what did not happen. No OOM killer fired. No cgroup limit applied,
because no slice constrained the tool. No userspace reclaim daemon existed to notice pressure
and act on it. And the session survived in the worst possible way: lege-comp and lege-shell both
stayed alive and both stayed unresponsive, so the desktop was present, not crashed, and offered
the user no route to the process eating the machine. A crash would have been recoverable in
seconds; forty-five minutes of a live but frozen session was not.

This is a first-party incident on the actual development machine, which is the machine LegeOS
is being built to run on and build itself on.

### There is no OpenURI backend interface to implement: the portal frontend owns OpenURI, and launches the handler outside LegeOS identity

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.openuri-is-the-frontends-portal/2` · scope `path "crates/lege-associationd/**"`, `path "portals/xdg-desktop-portal-lege/**"`

`org.freedesktop.impl.portal.OpenURI` does not exist. On the declared Ubuntu base, `xdg-desktop-portal 1.20.3+ds-1ubuntu1.1` knows 25 impl interfaces and OpenURI is not among them (`strings /usr/libexec/xdg-desktop-portal | grep 'impl.portal'`); no `/usr/share/dbus-1/interfaces/*OpenURI*` XML is installed; and none of the six installed backends (gtk, kde, cosmic, lxqt, kwallet, gnome-keyring) claims it. The frontend implements `org.freedesktop.portal.OpenURI` itself: it finds the default handler through GAppInfo and `mimeapps.list`, delegates only the 'which application' question to `org.freedesktop.impl.portal.AppChooser`, and then launches the chosen desktop entry in its own scope.

Two consequences for LegeOS, both live at this commit. First, the launch does not go through `Launcher1`, so a file opened from a browser is not started into a LegeOS cgroup; since identity comes from the cgroup by design, that process is anonymous to `AppIdentity1` and to every policy keyed on it. Second, `lege-associationd` regenerates its `mimeapps.list` export after every association mutation (`crates/lege-associationd/src/dbus.rs`) but nothing writes it at session start (`services/lege-sessiond/src/main.rs` wires `AssociationApi` without an initial export), so a fresh home — or one whose file was removed — can disagree with `Associations1` until something changes a default.

The portal backend was corrected to match this reality rather than to claim an OpenURI interface nothing would call: `legeos.portal` still claims exactly four interfaces, and the AppChooser leg was fixed to recognise a LegeOS canonical app id among the desktop file ids the frontend offers (`AppIdentity1.ListApplications`), which is what makes the LegeOS default actually win.

**supersedes** `@legeos.observation.openuri-is-the-frontends-portal/1` · **verified_by** `@legeos.evidence.stale-observation-triage-20260908/1`

> **Stale** — `watches "portals/xdg-desktop-portal-lege/**"` was matched by `8b2ae246`, which touched `portals/xdg-desktop-portal-lege/Cargo.toml`. ### A name-tag click deadlocked templar-comp: sync_after_change re-locked Smithay's pointer mutex inside the grab

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.pointer-grab-reentry-deadlocks-the-compositor/1`

templar-comp deadlocks its own main thread when the window model changes inside a pointer grab. Smithay 1ed69cb's PointerHandle::button and ::motion hold the pointer's std::sync::Mutex (PointerHandle.inner) while they call the active PointerGrab; WindowGestureGrab::button, on a name-tag press released without moving (pins_on_click), calls toggle_always_on_top -> space_sync::sync_after_change -> refresh_pointer_focus, which calls PointerHandle::is_grabbed and so locks that mutex a second time on the same thread. That lock never returns: no more frames, input or protocol dispatch, the main thread asleep in a futex at about 0 percent CPU, the kernel silent, every other process running. The same path runs when a dragged window is dropped on another's band (group_windows). It has been in every installed build since 6d7943f (2026-09-10, refresh_pointer_focus) together with 8b2ae24's pin-on-click, including b919ed4. Freeze 2026-10-01 boot fbbc3d53: the user clicked a window's tag after 11:44:23 UTC, the screen froze, and they pressed the power key at 11:45:30. The regression test backend::check::tests::changing_the_window_model_inside_a_pointer_grab_does_not_hang_the_compositor hangs (10 s timeout) on the old code and passes once sync_after_change queues the pointer refresh on the event loop's idle list instead of running it inline.

> **Stale** — `watches "compositor/templar-comp/src/space_sync.rs"` was matched by `c24c0c85`, which touched `compositor/templar-comp/src/space_sync.rs`. See [REVIEW-REQUIRED.md](REVIEW-REQUIRED.md#a-name-tag-click-deadlocked-templar-comp-sync_after_change-re-locked-smithays-pointer-mutex-inside-the-grab).

### A reconcile that finds nothing changed costs as much as one that finds a hundred changes, and both scale with the tree

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.reconciliation-cost-tracks-tree-size-not-change-size/3` · scope `path "crates/lege-file-index/src/mutation.rs"`, `path "crates/lege-file-index/src/reconcile.rs"`

Re-measured on a quiet machine at 2026-09-04 13:25, after every lane had stopped compiling. Recursive reconciliation with the change set held fixed and the tree grown, release build, warm page cache (read_bytes zero throughout, so these are best-case): 1,000 files / 1,540 entries took 16 ms to acquire, 21 ms to reconcile with nothing changed and 26 ms with 100 files changed; 10,000 files / 15,339 entries took 157 / 281 / 254 ms; 100,000 files / 153,327 entries took 1,867 ms to acquire, 3,240 ms with nothing changed and 3,375 ms with 100 files changed. The architectural conclusion is unchanged and is the point of the record: reconcile cost is proportional to tree size and essentially blind to how much actually changed, so it cannot serve as steady-state maintenance. By contrast Index::apply is now flat in tree size after the accelerator-index work: a warm single-mutation batch costs 0.2 ms at 15,339 entries and 0.3 ms at 153,327, against 2.7 ms and 41.9 ms before, and a 100-mutation batch at 153,327 entries costs 4.1 ms against 43.1 ms before. A crawl therefore costs roughly 790x a hundred-mutation batch at this size. This revision corrects revision 1, which recorded 32,838 ms acquisition and 39,594 ms no-change reconcile at 153,326 entries: those figures were about ten times too high because they were taken while four other lanes were compiling on the same machine. Removing the new accelerator index leaves the reconcile at 2,027 / 3,420 ms, confirming the correction is a quieter machine rather than the index work. Any figure in docs/measurements/btrfs-delta-2026-09-04.md derived from the original run is wrong by roughly an order of magnitude and should be read against this record.

**supersedes** `@legeos.observation.reconciliation-cost-tracks-tree-size-not-change-size/2` · **derived_from** `@legeos.work.adaptive-index-maintenance/1` · **verified_by** `@legeos.evidence.stale-observation-triage-20260908/1`

### Every shipped binary carries its line tables: the debs are ~5x their stripped size, deliberately, and the ISO will inherit that

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.release-debs-ship-unstripped-line-tables/2` · scope `path "Cargo.toml"`, `path "distro/iso/**"`, `path "distro/metapackages/**"`

`[profile.release]` sets `debug = "line-tables-only"` (Cargo.toml:139, present since the initial commit) so a panic backtrace off a real desktop names file:line rather than a hex address. `cargo deb` is told neither to strip nor to split symbols, so the byte-identical unstripped binary goes into the package: lege-hostd is 22.7 MB shipped against 4.5 MB stripped, and every deb in the set carries the same multiple. This is the accepted trade for the developer edition, not an oversight — the point is that a live ISO built from this archive will be several hundred MB larger than the same set stripped, and that is the expected size, not a fault to chase. Turning it off later is `separate-debug-symbols = true` under each `[package.metadata.deb]` (thirteen one-line additions), which keeps the line tables in a sidecar and ships the stripped binary; do that when medium size starts to matter, and expect the ISO to shrink sharply.

**supersedes** `@legeos.observation.release-debs-ship-unstripped-line-tables/1` · **derived_from** `@legeos.decision.debian-packaging/1` · **blocks** `@legeos.work.self-hosting-legeos/1` · **verified_by** `@legeos.evidence.stale-observation-triage-20260908/1`

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.search-arrays-answer-broad-queries-at-two-million-in-under-20ms/1` · scope `path "crates/templar-file-index/src/arrays.rs"`, `path "crates/templar-file-index/src/query.rs"`, `path "crates/templar-file-index/src/schema.rs"`, `path "tools/xtask/src/index_bench.rs"`

At 2,000,001 entries, first page of 100, p50/p95: `d` (1,999,968 matches) SQL 3,257/3,264 ms vs arrays 16.8/17.8 ms; `f1` (550,000) 1,169/1,171 vs 14.9/18.0 ms; `txt` (1,600,000) 1,728/1,737 vs 16.8/18.2 ms; `f12.txt` (50,000) 274/276 vs 10.7/11.9 ms; the path needle `d3/d4` stays on SQL at 688-710 ms. Building the arrays took 1.6 s at 2M rows and 60-83 ms at 90-99k. On a VACUUM INTO copy of the live home index (99,447 rows), arrays and SQL returned identical totals, ranks and order for 10 needles x 5 sorts x 2 directions (an earlier arrays build that assumed a directory's subtree follows it immediately in byte order produced 50 mismatches; `d-x` and `d.rs` sort between `d` and `d/`); `e` 234 ms SQL vs 2.4 ms arrays, `cargo` 28 vs 1.7 ms, `main.rs` 0.7 vs 1.4 ms. The SQL fallback for one- and two-character needles is slower than the old capped search (`e` 234 ms vs 126 ms) because it now counts and orders every match exactly.

### Index search costs about 1.3 µs per matched row, mostly row materialisation and ranking; a truncated candidate set is not the best N, and folder-scoped Search1 drops in-scope matches

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.search-cost-is-linear-in-matches-and-truncation-is-not-best-first/1` · scope `path "crates/templar-file-index/src/query.rs"`, `path "crates/templar-file-index/src/schema.rs"`, `path "services/templar-filed/src/search.rs"`

Measured 2026-10-01 on a VACUUM INTO copy of the live index (94,953 live entries under /home/dk, release build, throwaway harness outside the tree). Index::search cost is linear in matched candidates at about 1.3 µs per row: `e` (like-scan, 94,928 matches) takes p50 126 ms with candidate_limit 200,000 and 63 ms at the default 50,000; `cargo` (FTS5 trigram, 14,691 matches) takes 19.5 ms. For `cargo` the FTS5 rowid lookup is 2.1 ms, entry_id after the filters 5.8 ms, entry_id plus sort keys (name_fold, path_bytes, size, mtime) 7.6 ms, and all ENTRY_COLUMNS decoded 10.9 ms; the remaining ~8.6 ms is rank_of re-folding every name and sorting whole EntryRows. The candidate LIMIT is applied before ranking, so a truncated result is the first N rows in FTS/rowid order, not the best N. Files.Search1 (the shell's folder-scoped search, limit 50) fetches the global top 200 and filters by path prefix afterwards: `lib` scoped to the LegeOS checkout returned 21 of its 24 matches. Storage: the vacuumed index is 148.7 MiB, of which entries_fts_data plus entries_fts_content is 88 MiB (about 940 bytes per entry), because the trigram index covers path_display as well as the name and stores its own copy of both columns.

> **Stale** — `watches "crates/templar-file-index/src/query.rs"` was matched by `0de91aaa`, which touched `crates/templar-file-index/src/query.rs`. See [REVIEW-REQUIRED.md](REVIEW-REQUIRED.md#index-search-costs-about-13-µs-per-matched-row-mostly-row-materialisation-and-ranking-a-truncated-candidate-set-is-not-the-best-n-and-folder-scoped-search1-drops-in-scope-matches).

### Session time enters sessiond at four edges and leaves by one broadcast

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.session-time-enters-sessiond-at-four-edges/1`

Nothing in lege-sessiond knew when its own session began, was locked, was unlocked, or went to
sleep. There was no logind signal match anywhere in the repository, and Lifecycle1.Lock only
emitted LockRequested. So anything meant to age with use had wall-clock time and nothing else,
which is wrong in exactly the case that matters: a laptop asleep for a week aged nothing, and a
screen locked overnight aged nothing.

Session time now enters the process at four points and leaves it by one. The four are:
sessiond's own startup (Started, sent last in main so every in-process subscriber is already
listening); Lifecycle1.Lock (Locked - the request, not a covered screen, because sessiond speaks
no Wayland and cannot observe the latter); Lifecycle1.NotifyUnlocked, which only
lege-shell.service may call because ext-session-lock-v1's unlock_and_destroy is the only thing
that clears a lock and the shell is the only process that calls it (Unlocked); and one match
rule on org.freedesktop.login1.Manager.PrepareForSleep, no polling (Sleeping(bool)).

The one exit is a tokio broadcast of SessionEdge, capacity 64. The Lifecycle1 signals
SessionStarted/Locked/Unlocked/Sleeping are a *view* of that channel, re-emitted by a single
relay task that subscribes to it - so a client watching the bus and a host counting in-process
cannot disagree about what happened, and no edge can reach the bus twice by two routes.

Two ceilings are deliberate. Locked fires at request time, so a lock the compositor refuses
closes the interval early - the shell tears that attempt down through the same release_lock
path, which reports Unlocked, so the error is bounded to one frame rather than an open
interval. And a session that cannot reach the system bus counts sleep as ordinary idle time;
it says so once in the log and otherwise runs unchanged, which is the same bargain SystemLogind
already makes for the power controls.

### Everything a terminal starts is the terminal: identity is the launch unit's cgroup, there is no workload, and the governor sees only Templar launch units

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.terminal-workloads-inherit-the-terminal-identity/1`

At 50af378. Launcher1 starts an application as app-templaros-<AppId>@<uuid>.service in app.slice via StartTransientUnit (crates/templar-appd/src/systemd1.rs:75-150, crates/templar-types/src/unit.rs:11-44), and AppIdentity1 resolves PID -> /proc/PID/cgroup -> deepest registered instance -> AppId (crates/templar-appd/src/identity.rs:125-180). cgroup membership is inherited at fork, so kitty -> bash -> cargo -> rustc are all kitty's instance; a GUI app started from that terminal resolves to the terminal with VerifiedLaunchClaimMismatch (identity.rs:162-176). Nothing in resourced knows a workload, build or terminal job; its scan only discovers app-templaros-* units (services/templar-resourced/src/scan.rs:41-66) and its own test ignores an app-flatpak-*.scope (:82), and its actions are per instance (cgroup.kill, memory.oom.group). background.slice is configured but nothing is placed in it. The garden's bash PROMPT_COMMAND hook (session/profile.d/60-templaros-garden.sh) is the one per-command hook a Templar terminal already has. AppProvenance.sandboxed is reported and not acted on (crates/templar-types/src/variant.rs:215-273).

### Four packages a laptop needs for sound and Wi-Fi authentication reach the image only through a Recommends

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.the-hardware-packages-that-matter-most-arrive-only-through-recommends/2` · scope `path "distro/iso/build.sh"`, `path "distro/seeds/selection.toml"`

The pinned closure's own no-recommends experiment lists firmware-sof-signed, wpasupplicant, alsa-ucm-conf and thermald among the 415 packages that disappear if Recommends are ever turned off: NetworkManager only Recommends wpasupplicant and wireless-regdb, and thermald is a Recommends of linux-image-generic. By contrast intel-microcode, amd64-microcode, wireless-regdb and every linux-firmware-* subpackage are hard Depends of linux-image-generic and need no declaration. The four Recommends-only names are now declared in the hardware layer with reasons; the hard-depended ones deliberately are not. distro/iso/build.sh sets Apt::Install-Recommends true, so today's medium gets them either way — the seed lines are what survives a policy change.

### nvidia-kernel-common's postinst fails inside an unshared bootstrap chroot, so the live medium carries no NVIDIA driver

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.the-nvidia-lrm-cannot-be-installed-in-an-unshared-bootstrap-chroot/2` · scope `path "distro/iso/build.sh"`, `path "installer/provision.sh"`

Bootstrapping the medium with legeos-nvidia-open in the include list fails the whole apt transaction: nvidia-kernel-common-580's postinst runs update-initramfs before initramfs-tools has been configured, and with no kernel version of its own it falls back to `uname -r` — the BUILD HOST's 6.17.0-41-generic — producing "/usr/sbin/mkinitramfs: .: cannot open /etc/initramfs-tools/initramfs.conf" and taking eleven NVIDIA packages down with it. distro/iso/build.sh therefore no longer includes legeos-nvidia-open: the live session runs on whatever KMS driver the kernel binds (the Intel iGPU on the reference laptop), and the NVIDIA LRM is installed into the target by installer/provision.sh, where there is a real /boot and a configured initramfs. The same failure mode is a risk for the provisioner's own `apt-get install legeos-kernel legeos-nvidia-open` in its chroot; P3.3 in QEMU is where that gets tested.

### A provisioned machine had no /etc/fstab, and its boot identity was a label every LegeOS disk shares

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.the-provisioner-wrote-no-fstab-at-all/2`

`installer/provision.sh` never wrote `/etc/fstab`: the word does not appear anywhere under `installer/`, `distro/` or `session/`. The mounts it makes are for the chroot and were never recorded, so a provisioned machine had nothing telling it how to mount @home, @var, @snapshots, @deployments or the ESP on its own. Separately, boot identity was `root=LABEL=legeos-root`, hardcoded in `boot_entries.rs:43` and `deploy.rs:128` — the same string on every LegeOS disk, so a machine with two attached mounts whichever the kernel enumerated first. This was scoped as a label-to-UUID migration; it was a missing step plus a migration.

### The booted system root is read-write, three routes run apt against it in place, and its dpkg database lives in the shared @var

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.the-system-root-is-mutable-in-place-and-its-package-database-lives-in-var/1`

At 50af378. The deployment command line is rootflags=subvol=@ rw (distro/deploy/layout.toml:97) and fstab mounts / from subvol=@ (installer/provision.sh, fstab block around :1219); the first known-good deployment is @ itself (provision.sh around :1481). apt changes that root in place by three routes: the provisioner's chrooted apt-get (provision.sh :1333-1402), templar dev deploy's pinned apt-get install --allow-downgrades on the live / (cli/templar/src/dev/install.rs:110-120), and the owner, whom scripts/update-templaros.sh:44-46 tells to run sudo apt-get upgrade for inherited packages. hostd's own transaction does it the intended way (snapshot, apt-get --root into the candidate, seal read-only: services/templar-hostd/src/updates.rs:280-313, apt.rs:63-84). /var is the separate @var subvolume (provision.sh fstab), so /var/lib/dpkg — the record of what is installed in @ — lives outside @ and outside any snapshot of it; hostd reads it from apt_root/var/lib/dpkg/status (services/templar-hostd/src/state.rs:209,225). [INFERENCE] after a rollback to an older @, the shared dpkg database still describes the newer one. No document states that OS updates must not touch /home; that holds only because @home is its own subvolume, and hostd does reach into @home for file-index checkpoints (services/templar-hostd/src/index_checkpoint.rs:96, polkit allow_active).

### The reference laptop has one 55.9 GiB free tail, a 100 MiB ESP, and a provisioner that only takes a whole disk

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.this-machines-partition-table-cannot-hold-legeos-as-it-stands/2` · scope `path "distro/**"`, `path "installer/**"`

Measured on the reference laptop. nvme0n1 (953.9 GiB) holds NTFS 536G, NTFS 949M, Lubuntu's ext4 root 416G with 8.7G free, the 100 MiB ESP and a 16 MiB partition, leaving a 0.5 GiB free tail. nvme1n1 (931.5 GiB) holds a 16 MiB partition and the 875.6 GiB NTFS projects partition, leaving 55.9 GiB unallocated at its tail. Three consequences. (1) The only place a LegeOS root can go without destroying Lubuntu or Windows is that 55.9 GiB tail, which fits a 1 GiB ESP and a ~54 GiB btrfs root but not a 42 GiB target directory. (2) distro/deploy/layout.toml requires an ESP of 512M-1G and the existing one is 100 MiB, sandwiched between Lubuntu's root and a 16 MiB partition, so a second ESP on nvme1n1 is the answer rather than growing it. (3) installer/provision.sh runs sgdisk --zap-all on its target and has no mode that consumes free space beside existing partitions, so it cannot be run on this machine at all as it stands. Separately: five Cargo path dependencies point outside the repository, so a LegeOS installation could not rebuild LegeOS; mmdebstrap and debootstrap are not installed on this host; and nm-tray-2 is neither packaged nor named in the seed declaration.

**supersedes** `@legeos.observation.this-machines-partition-table-cannot-hold-legeos-as-it-stands/1` · **verified_by** `@legeos.evidence.stale-observation-triage-20260908/1`

### Omarchy launches applications into transient systemd units too, then identifies windows by self-declared app_id anyway

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.transient-unit-launch-converged-independently/2` · scope `path "crates/lege-appd/**"`, `path "crates/lege-types/**"`

Basecamp's Omarchy independently arrived at the same launch primitive LegeOS uses: bin/omarchy-launch-browser and five sibling scripts start applications with `systemd-run --user --collect --unit="omarchy-browser-$(date +%s%N)"`, giving one transient unit and therefore one cgroup per launch. It then does not use it. There is no reference to a cgroup, a unit or /proc/<pid>/cgroup anywhere under shell/; the shell identifies windows purely from the client's self-declared app_id (12 references). The cgroup exists and the information is discarded. This sharpens what LegeOS's identity model actually contributes: not that a per-launch cgroup exists, but that naming it app-legeos-<AppId>@<InstanceId>.service makes the cgroup name carry the identity, so a window's PID resolves to a cgroup, the cgroup name resolves to an AppId, and the governor, the dock and the notification router all key off one fact nobody had to ask the client for. Omarchy's unit name is a timestamp and carries no identity, so it cannot make that journey even though it has the cgroup. Independent convergence on the primitive is evidence the primitive is right; the naming convention is the part that turns it into an identity system, and is the part to defend in review.

**supersedes** `@legeos.observation.transient-unit-launch-converged-independently/1`

### Ubuntu 26.04 has no linux-modules-extra; it splits linux-firmware per vendor and lifts some drivers into linux-modules-<name>-generic packages of their own

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.ubuntu-2604-splits-firmware-and-modules-into-per-vendor-packages/2` · scope `path "distro/seeds/selection.toml"`, `path "docs/measurements/hardware-inventory-*"`

Checked against the pinned snapshot's file->package index (https://snapshot.ubuntu.com/ubuntu/20260905T011226Z/dists/resolute/Contents-amd64.gz): resolute ships ONE linux-modules-<ver>-generic — there is no linux-modules-extra-generic to seed, and every module the reference laptop loads (rtw89_8852ce, i915, btusb, btrtl, snd-hda-intel, snd-hda-scodec-cs35l41, cs-dsp, nvme) is in it. What 26.04 does instead is lift particular drivers OUT into their own flavour-tracking packages — linux-modules-iwlwifi-generic (Intel Wi-Fi), and linux-main-modules-{ipu6,ipu7,zfs,usbio,evdi,v4l2loopback,doca-ofed}-<ver>-generic — none of which linux-image-generic depends on. linux-firmware is likewise now a metapackage over linux-firmware-{realtek,intel-graphics,intel-misc,misc,nvidia-graphics,...}, all pulled by hard Depends. Consequences for the medium: an Intel-Wi-Fi laptop has no radio unless linux-modules-iwlwifi-generic is declared (it now is), and the reference laptop's own firmware — rtw89/rtw8852c_fw-2.bin and rtl_bt/* in linux-firmware-realtek, i915/adlp_* in linux-firmware-intel-graphics, the cirrus/cs35l41 speaker-amp blobs in linux-firmware-misc, regulatory.db in wireless-regdb — is all provided, with zero firmware in use unprovided. Three loaded modules have no resolute package and none is a hardware gap: blake2b_generic and polyval_clmulni were renamed (blake2b, libpolyval), lenovo_wmi_capdata01 became lenovo-wmi-capdata, and legion_laptop is an out-of-tree DKMS module on the development host.

**supersedes** `@legeos.observation.ubuntu-2604-splits-firmware-and-modules-into-per-vendor-packages/1` · **derived_from** `@legeos.decision.base-ubuntu-2604-kernel-70/1` · **verified_by** `@legeos.evidence.stale-observation-triage-20260908/1`

### Unprivileged fanotify is one mark per directory, arms 2.5x slower than inotify and costs about twice the memory, for 6.4% more headroom

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.unprivileged-fanotify-costs-more-per-directory-than-inotify/2` · scope `path "crates/lege-fanotify/**"`, `path "crates/lege-file-index/src/watch.rs"`

Measured on the reference laptop (kernel 6.17, ext4, uid 1000, no capabilities) over 100,000 directories, three runs, spread under 3%: inotify arms at 0.8-0.9 us per directory, fanotify inode marks at 2.1-2.2 us. Kernel SUnreclaim per directory is 104-106 B for inotify and 78-81 B for fanotify; process VmRSS per directory is 68 B for inotify and 287 B for fanotify, because every fanotify event in fid mode names its directory by opaque file handle and open_by_handle_at(2) is EPERM without CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH, so the handle-to-path map must live in userspace at one entry per directory. Totals: ~172 B per directory for inotify against ~366 B for fanotify. Against the kernel ceiling, 189,089 directories are 75.6% of fs.inotify.max_user_watches (250,074) and 71.1% of fs.fanotify.max_user_marks (266,105) — 6.4% more headroom where a home root needs 51% more than the index's WatchBudget. On throughput the two are indistinguishable: identical raw event counts and kinds for a create+write workload (40,000 events from 40,000 operations) and for a cargo-build-shaped create+write+rename+delete burst (100,000 events from 80,000 operations), within 2% on delivery rate, and both overflow at exactly 16,385 events with nothing reading the fd. Unprivileged fanotify also requires a fid-reporting mode: FAN_CLASS_NOTIF with no fid flags, FAN_UNLIMITED_QUEUE, FAN_MARK_MOUNT and FAN_MARK_FILESYSTEM are all EPERM.

**supersedes** `@legeos.observation.unprivileged-fanotify-costs-more-per-directory-than-inotify/1` · **verified_by** `@legeos.evidence.stale-observation-triage-20260908/1`

### On the installed TemplarOS, home plus the project drive need about 0.91x of the index's inotify watch budget, so watcher exhaustion is no longer the expected outcome

`verified` · `@legeos.observation.watch-budget-fits-home-and-project-drive-on-templaros/2` · scope `path "crates/templar-file-index/src/watch.rs"`

Measured on the installed TemplarOS (reference laptop, /home on btrfs @home) on 2026-10-01 with `cargo run -q -p xtask --release -- index-bench dirs`, which counts through the index's own RootPolicy: /home/dk holds 6,445 directories after the skip list, and /mnt/second (the NTFS project drive, ntfs-3g fuseblk) holds 110,258. fs.inotify.max_user_watches is 257,001, so WatchBudget is 128,500; fanotify max_user_marks is 273,909. Home alone needs 0.05x the budget, the project drive 0.86x, and both together about 0.91x, so on this machine neither root nor their sum exhausts the watch budget. The 2026-09-04 premise (189,089 home directories plus 172,681 on the project drive) described the old Lubuntu home and does not hold here; it returns only if the old home is migrated wholesale or another large root is added.

**supersedes** `@legeos.observation.watch-budget-fits-home-and-project-drive-on-templaros/1`

## Assessments

### Astra advisor review of the memory governor, the watcher host and the file-index core — nine ranked findings, four must-fix

`verified` · `@legeos.assessment.astra-memory-polling-indexing-review-20260909/1` · scope `path "crates/lege-file-index/**"`, `path "services/lege-filed/src/delta_catchup.rs"`, `path "services/lege-filed/src/index_host.rs"`, `path "services/lege-filed/src/observer.rs"`, `path "services/lege-filed/src/watcher.rs"`, `path "services/lege-resourced/**"`

An independent advisor pass (packet ad-9afae8b350d5, result rs-9198dc49c727, filed 2026-09-09 before the parent's notes were revealed) read every in-scope production file in lege-resourced, lege-filed's watcher/observer/index_host/delta_catchup and lege-file-index, ran the scoped tests (359 pass, 9 ignored) and scoped clippy (clean), and ranked nine findings. The parent's four hypotheses held: unbounded handoff channels, un-deduplicated repair queueing, a snapshot that is not one read transaction, and a failed PSI descriptor that degrades to a spin or a 60 s sleep. Astra added three independent priority defects: the governor's fallback wait keeps the 60 s idle heartbeat with no usable trigger and arms session.slice while governed instances live in the sibling app.slice; a complete subtree repair pass upgrades a root to Current/complete and erases an older whole-root overflow, watch-exhaustion or incomplete-namespace reason; and the watcher drops a failed coalesced apply batch with only a warning and can repair before a queued overflow Invalidate has settled, so the later invalidation re-stales a freshly repaired root with no work queued. Two further P2 items (unbounded D-Bus signal backlog and a count-bounded, not byte-bounded, trace ring; a critical-pressure grace delay bound to the episode rather than the victim, so a new victim can be killed on its first selected tick) and two deferred redesigns (btrfs delta baseline/checkpoint atomicity and watch rearming; Index::children decoding the whole descendant range with parent_id not maintained on move) complete the set. All findings are code-path analysis backed by passing tests; no production workload timing, privileged PSI trigger, D-Bus saturation or btrfs fault injection was measured.

- `#btrfs-baseline` — delta_catchup.rs returns without a baseline and ensure_baseline has no production caller; plant writes the baseline pointer before decode/apply succeeds; btrfs_delta.rs reads the stream with unbounded read_to_end.
- `#children-scan` — lib.rs Index::children decodes the whole descendant range and filters in Rust; take-on-trust reconciliation leaves parent None and place_at does not update parent_id on move.
- `#critical-grace` — policy.rs critical_steps keeps one critical_since per pressure episode, not per selected victim.
- `#governor-wake` — daemon.rs run_loop arms a PSI trigger on session.slice while scan.rs governs app.slice, and while Normal always waits the 60 s IDLE_HEARTBEAT even when PressureWait has no trigger; Trigger::wait maps POLLERR/HUP/NVAL and non-EINTR errors to Timeout.
- `#resourced-bounds` — daemon.rs hands signals to the D-Bus task over an unbounded channel; trace.rs bounds the ring by record count (5000), not bytes.
- `#snapshot-frame` — snapshot.rs write_snapshot reads generation, change sequence, roots and each root's entries through separate pooled reads despite documenting one read transaction, and buffers the full payload in RAM.
- `#subtree-upgrade` — generation.rs committed_state derives Current/complete from the scoped pass alone; the metadata axis guards subtree upgrades but the namespace axis does not.
- `#unbounded-handoff` — watch.rs opens an unbounded mpsc channel from the inotify reader thread and drains it whole per poll; watcher.rs repairs is a LIFO Vec with duplicates.
- `#watcher-ordering` — watcher.rs drops a failed coalesced apply batch with a warning and queues no repair; an overflow repair can run before its Invalidate mutation leaves the coalescer.

### Desktop test-readiness audit — strong logic tests, missing system validation and core interaction surfaces

`verified` · `@legeos.assessment.desktop-test-readiness-20260827/1` · scope `path "apps/**"`, `path "ci/**"`, `path "compositor/**"`, `path "portals/**"`, `path "scripts/**"`, `path "services/**"`, `path "shell/**"`, `path "tests/**"`

LegeOS has a large, currently green unit/property test base, but the desktop cannot yet be considered system-tested: the integration harness does not start or drive a real composed session, the documented hardware runner is inert, installation/greeter/recovery/hardware paths remain manual, and several ordinary desktop interactions still have no graphical implementation.

- `#accessibility-and-localisation` — The repository ships accessibility and localisation intentions, but no AT-SPI/accessibility-tree implementation or runtime Fluent loader is present in the audited sources.
- `#automated-foundation` — All 1,015 workspace tests, lint/format checks, runtime smoke, and seven structural/action gates pass on the audited working tree.
- `#desktop-capability-gaps` — Graphical Settings is still a text renderer; FileChooser, AppChooser and Background portal prompts use NoUiAvailable; session lock is NotSupported; notifications are stored but not rendered; and power profiles are stored without idle/lid/brightness/battery actuation.
- `#false-green-risks` — The smoke test imports developer-host application state and tolerates an UNHEALTHY boot-health report, Home's offscreen test checks PNG validity and dimensions rather than rendered pixels, CI builds only the sessiond Debian package, and compositor-active boot health is explicitly unwired.
- `#hardware-runner-noop` — `lege doctor --hardware` produces byte-identical output to ordinary doctor because Context.hardware is never consumed; tests/hardware/*.toml is currently passive checklist data.
- `#system-test-gap` — There is no automated greetd-to-Home login, nested compositor input/render interaction, installed multi-package session, VM first-boot, shell-death recovery, or real-hardware execution path.
